item.title: [The Boston Globe] Pedro Martinez on Game 7 in 2003, no regrets on calling the Yankees his daddy, and a mission to help - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Dan Shaughnessy

item.content:encoded:
Many of us believe he’s the best pitcher we’ve ever seen. He’s a blue-chip, first-ballot Hall of Famer, part of the Red Sox team that broke the Curse, and seen on TBS after Sox playoff games in any given October. He’ll be 55 next month and spends every year shuttling between Boston and his native Dominican Republic, when he’s not working in Atlanta. He has no regrets about saying “The Yankees are my daddy,” all those years ago, and he thinks the Red Sox have a shot to beat the Yankees in New York next week.
He is the one and only Pedro Martinez, and he’s spending Thursday in Lawrence with his wife, Carolina, launching an after-school coding program at South Lawrence East Elementary School, then engaging in a question-and-answer session with hundreds of students at Lawrence High School.
“Lawrence has been kind of forgotten a little bit,” said Martinez. “It has gotten kind of old in front of our eyes, but there is so much need. If there’s something I can really identify myself with, it is need. I grew up in those kind of needs. I’m just expressing the cry I had when I was a kid. I get excited every time I see a kid that has an opportunity to become someone.”
Martinez’s new program is designed to bridge resource gaps and enhance classroom learning for young students across Lawrence. His foundation, dedicated to transforming the lives of youth in the United States and the Dominican Republic, was started in 1998 when he joined the Sox after five-plus stellar seasons with the Dodgers and Expos.
“I got a very pleasant surprise when I got to Fenway as soon as I saw the drums and the people with the [Dominican] flag and the atmosphere kind of changing,” Martinez recalled. “Mayor [Thomas] Menino was kind enough to take me in his SUV to give me a tour around Boston, and right away I fell in love with the people … and the Latino community all over the place, and that’s when I landed in Lawrence, Lynn, Dorchester, and all those areas that continue to be linked to me.”
It was in those early Boston days that Martinez’s Fenway mound starts “became the curfew back home in the Dominican every time I pitched.”
A connection was made; an ongoing, lasting relationship because of the Pedro Martinez Foundation.
In 2026, Martinez and teammate/countryman David Ortiz are listed as “special assistants” in the fourth line of the the Red Sox’ official front office directory, just below chief baseball officer Craig Breslow. Martinez occasionally helps young Sox pitchers at spring training, but he was out of the loop when the decision was made to fire manager Alex Cora and six coaches just 27 games into the season.
“I was actually talking to Alex a couple of days before,” Martinez remembered. “When I found out, I wasn’t angry, I just couldn’t understand how everything snowballed to that point.”
Martinez’s beloved former teammate, catcher/captain Jason Varitek, was part of the purge. The Sox claimed Varitek was “reassigned,” but he hasn’t surfaced anywhere in the organization.
Does Martinez think the burned bridge will be repaired?
“I think it’s going to be OK with Jason,” said the three-time Cy Young Award winner. “Jason is a very professional person. He understands that business part, just like Alex Cora.”
What does Martinez think about the local demonization of Rafael Devers?
“This is a very misunderstood kid,” he said. “Devers is very shy. But he is legit. He’s a guy that doesn’t know how to express himself and has a hard time trusting anybody but his father. His father knows the actual truth … Devers is very respectful, a very lovely kid, but now it’s over and the team is on its way to success. … You have to learn to love Boston if you want to survive in Boston. Boston is 24/7 talking about their sports.”
Does Martinez want Payton Tolle or Sonny Gray starting Game 1?
“You don’t go wrong with either one,” he said. “Sonny is a true professional, a true competitor. I love, love Tolle. Just his amazing attitude. I love every single pitch he throws. I love everything about him.
“The Yankees are vulnerable, especially without [Aaron] Judge. I don’t think the Red Sox are intimidated by the Yankees. I think they can beat not only the Yankees but any team in baseball.”
The highlight of Martinez’s baseball career?
“Being part of the 25 that brought the trophy to Boston.”
Ever wish he never said, “The Yankees are my daddy”?
“No. I was being honest. That’s what you guys demand from all of us. The Yankees had my number at that point, and I expressed it. I will tell you in the most honest way, I got my ass kicked.”
Which brings us back to 2003, when Grady Little was fired (almost immediately) after failing to take Martinez out of the game when Pedro was past his pitch limit after seven innings of Game 7 of the ALCS at Yankee Stadium. Martinez had fanned Alfonso Soriano on his final pitch of the seventh, was at 100 pitches, and believed he was done for the night.
“[Red Sox pitching coach] Dave Wallace told me I was done after, so I didn’t put my jacket on,” said Martinez. “I had looked up in the sky and gave thanks to God for the seven innings I pitched. Our bullpen was lights out. All of a sudden Grady was like, ‘I don’t like [Alan] Embree against Nick Johnson in the eighth.’ He said, ‘You give me Nick Johnson and I got the rest of the bullpen for you.’ That’s the true story.”
Back on the mound, leading, 5-2, in the eighth, Martinez retired Johnson on a second-pitch popup to start the inning, then looked to the dugout. Nobody moved.
“Nothing happened,” recalled Martinez. “So I just kept going. I gave up a couple of line drives, and everything just snowballed after that. I thought I made a great pitch on [Jorge] Posada, but Posada blooped it [for a two-run double].”
All in all, it was four straight hits and a tie game before Little finally pulled Martinez after 23 disastrous eighth-inning pitches. Then Aaron Boone (now the Yankees’ manager) happened in the 11th.
Two summers ago, Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin wrote President Joe Biden a letter, imploring America’s tiring leader to end his reelection campaign. As part of his logic, Raskin compared Biden’s career to Martinez’s Game 7 performance, writing that there is “no shame in taking a well-deserved bow … when your arm is tired out.”
Days later, Biden pulled out of the race.
“I don’t know what to tell you about that,” chuckled Martinez. “Grady just told me, ‘Get one more out.’ That was Nick Johnson, right?”
Right.
All these years later, the wounds have healed and Martinez is on a greater mission, taking his message to Lawrence.
“I don’t have enough words to describe how grateful I am to have my opportunity through baseball and make a difference now,” said Martinez. “My message to these kids in Lawrence is that nothing in life is too far away if you have the will, if you have the passion.”
Dan Shaughnessy is a Globe columnist. He can be reached at daniel.shaughnessy@globe.com. Follow him @dan_shaughnessy.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are in the middle of a series with the Tampa Bay Rays, but they’ve already clinched a postseason spot, which is set to begin next week.
It seems they just about know exactly what seed they’ll have and who they’ll play as well.
One Tampa Bay win over New York would clinch the AL East for the Rays, which would then slot the Yankees as the top Wild Card team and, as of right now, have them hosting a best-of-three series against the Boston Red Sox next week.
Yankees Will Likely Be Without Judge
Prior to Tuesday’s doubleheader, Yankees manager Aaron Boone revealed that he does not expect Judge to return for the Wild Card series next week due to his calf injury.
He received an injection in his calf this week, and the diagnosis was a moderate calf strain.
“We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone said.
Aaron Judge is likely out for the AL Wild Card Series vs. Boston. “We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Aaron Boone said.
Judge had a PPP injection in his right calf during the off-day.
— Bryan Hoch ⚾️ (@BryanHoch) September 22, 2026
This now makes it all the more important for the Yankees’ depleted offense to have their starting rotation hold down the fort, which it has done all season long, headlined by Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodon, Max Fried, and Will Warren.
Pedro Martinez Makes Suggestion for Yankees
One of the biggest questions facing the Yankees is how they plan to structure a shortened rotation come playoff time, and Hall of Fame pitcher and MLB on TBS analyst Pedro Martinez believes he knows exactly how they should use their core pitchers.
“For the Yankees’ pitching rotation, I’d go with Schlittler first, Rodon second, and Cole third,” Martinez posted on X.
For the Yankees’ pitching rotation, I’d go with Schlittler first, Rodón second, and Cole third. #mlbontbs
— Pedro Martinez (@45PedroMartinez) September 22, 2026
You’re not going to pitch all five starters. That’s just not realistic. With the potential for more off days, you’re going to want your best arms available.
While Schlittler is an obvious no-brainer. Boone will have to decide whether he wants to go with a three-man group or extend it to four and have both Rodon and Fried start, rather than moving one of them to the bullpen alongside Warren, which seems like the most likely outcome for now.

item.content:encoded:
As we make our way through the final week of the regular season, there doesn't seem to be much suspense as to who will be named MVP. At least, that's what we can glean from our latest -- and final -- MLB.com 2026 MVP poll.
Yordan Alvarez is still well out in front in the American League despite relatively mediocre production of late. In the National League, Pete Crow-Armstrong is wrapping up one of the best all-around seasons in recent memory.
Thirty-eight MLB.com experts cast votes for who they think will earn MVP honors after this season, with 32 players receiving at least one vote. As a reminder, votes were based not only on results so far, but also on how things are expected to play out the rest of the season.
Voters ranked their top five picks in each league on a 5-4-3-2-1 scale -- five points for a first-place vote, four points for a second-place vote and so on. Here are the results.
All stats are through Sunday unless otherwise noted.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
Alvarez has been so good this year that what qualifies as a slump for him would be a good stretch for most other hitters. Over his past 41 games, he is hitting .264 with an .840 OPS. Again, not bad for most, but well below the standard of the AL leader in average (.313) and OPS (1.027). Alvarez has three homers and five RBIs through 16 games this month, leaving him tied with the O's Pete Alonso and one home run behind the Rays' Junior Caminero for the AL lead and nine RBIs behind Alonso for the top spot in that statistic. Even though his Triple Crown chances have faded, Alvarez has still put together an awesome 2026 at the plate. His 179 wRC+ is at least 27 points better than any other qualified hitter.
We know Caminero is one of the game's great sluggers. He is finishing up his second straight 40-homer season and swings harder than anyone. But what's been most impressive about his season is his improved strike-zone judgment. He has upped his walk rate from a below-average 6.3% to 11.5%, which ranks in the 80th percentile of MLB. He's also maintained a very solid strikeout rate (18.5%). He's not chasing as much, has shaved his whiff rate and is making more contact overall. That blend of patience, power and bat control is a special combination, especially in a 23-year-old player. Carrying a .363 on-base percentage (52 points better than last season), Caminero's .892 OPS ranks third in the AL.
Witt has had better offensive seasons, although 18 homers, 43 steals and a 119 wRC+ in 137 games is not too shabby. But when you consider his entire skill set, Witt remains extremely valuable. His +16 fielding run value is tied for third in the Majors, and his 22 outs above average tops the AL. He also has a +8 baserunning run value, one behind the D-backs' Corbin Carroll for the MLB lead. So while he hasn't been as undeniable in the batter's box as he was in 2024 (169 wRC+), Witt's all-around greatness has him atop the AL FanGraphs WAR leaderboard (6.6) and in line for a possible top-five finish in the MVP voting for the third time in three years.
There has been quite a bit of MVP chatter surrounding Schlittler in recent weeks. And why not? He is pacing the AL in ERA (1.94), WHIP (0.91) and FanGraphs pitching WAR (6.1). He ranks second in the junior circuit in opponents' batting average (.182) and strikeout-minus-walk rate (25.0%). He has allowed one or zero runs in 21 starts. That's a Yankees franchise record and something only two other pitchers age-25 or younger have accomplished in the Live Ball Era (since 1920): Blake Snell (2018) and Dean Chance (1964). He seems like a lock for the AL Cy Young Award at this point, but Schlittler will receive his fair share of MVP love.
Schlittler hasn't been the only indispensable Yankee this year. While New York has been without Aaron Judge for a large portion of the season and has missed other star bats as well due to injuries, Rice has been a constant. He ranks third in the AL in homers (39) and runs scored (100). He's fourth in the league in RBIs (95) and OPS (.888), and tied for fourth in batting run value (+34). With two homers during the final week, Rice would become just the second non-Judge Yankee over the past decade to hit at least 41 homers in a season, joining Juan Soto (2024).
Others receiving votes: Willson Contreras, Red Sox; Pete Alonso, Orioles; Kevin McGonigle, Tigers; Miguel Vargas, White Sox; Randy Arozarena, Mariners; Munetaka Murakami, White Sox; Dylan Cease, Blue Jays
NATIONAL LEAGUE
Last month, PCA jumped over Ohtani and into the No. 1 spot in our poll. This month, he has run away from the rest of the field. The recipient of every first-place vote cast by our panel, Crow-Armstrong is tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead in home runs (45). No one has more runs (118), extra-base hits (83) or total bases (351) this season. With 38 steals, the Cubs' dynamic center fielder could become the seventh member of the 40-40 club later this week. Oh, and let's not overlook the fact that he is arguably the best defensive player at any position right now. It's no longer a question of whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP. The award is as good as his right now. But will he win it in unanimous fashion?
Ohtani remains the clear runner-up in the NL despite playing in just three games this month due to his nagging left knee and right biceps injuries. The good news is Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said "there's a good chance" Ohtani will be activated from the 15-day injured list Wednesday after a minimum stint. He won't pitch for the rest of the season, leaving him with a 1.79 ERA and 95 K's over 85 2/3 innings. But Ohtani will have a few games to add to his offensive totals (30 homers, 142 wRC+).
We mentioned earlier how Schlittler looks like the heavy favorite for the AL Cy Young Award. Misiorowski is an even bigger shoo-in in the senior circuit. Through 169 1/3 innings, Miz leads the Majors in just about every category, including ERA (1.86), WHIP (0.80), strikeout-minus-walk rate (31.7%) and fWAR (6.5), to name just a few. Opposing batters have a scant .474 OPS against Misiorowski, which is the second-lowest by any qualified starter in the Divisional Era (since 1969). Pedro Martinez, in one of the greatest seasons by a pitcher, recorded a .473 opponents' OPS in 2000.
De La Cruz, who didn't receive a single vote in our previous MVP poll, has been red-hot for Cincinnati over the past month. In his last 27 games, he is batting .404 with eight homers, six steals and a 1.205 OPS. He collected multiple hits in 14 of those games, and his 2.5 fWAR during this period is the best in the big leagues. This prolonged hot streak has given De La Cruz a career-best 139 wRC+ and has left him two homers and two steals away from becoming the fourth Red in the 30-30 club and the first since Brandon Phillips in 2007.
Schwarber has fallen into a bit of a rut, going 4-for-34 with one home run over his past 10 games. He's also eight strikeouts away from setting a new record for K's in a single season. Even so, you have to admire Schwarber's consistency. He will end up with more than 40 homers and 150 games played in four of the past five seasons. He has surpassed 100 walks for a fourth consecutive season, and a third NL home run title is right there for the taking, too.
Others receiving votes: Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres; Brice Turang, Brewers; Matt Olson, Braves; James Wood, Nationals; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Alex Bregman, Cubs; Bryce Harper, Phillies; Jake Bauers, Brewers; Otto Lopez, Marlins; Gabriel Moreno, Diamondbacks; Rafael Devers, Giants; Alec Burleson, Cardinals; CJ Abrams, Nationals; Corbin Carroll, Diamondbacks; Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies

item.content:encoded:
If you're not already a card collector, Red Sox fans, here's the quick version of what product sports cards enthusiasts are going crazy over right now. Bowman Chrome is Topps' flagship prospect release, the one product every year built specifically around getting a player's first-ever card into the hobby before he's played a single big-league game. Think of it like a company's IPO. It's the first moment the public gets to invest or collect a piece of a player’s career, before anyone really knows what it'll become.
That's the appeal, and it's also the risk. Some of these names turn into stars. Some never sniff the majors at all. Either way, this is the top of the sports card market right now, and some of these prices have gotten astronomical. You have to truly believe in these prospects to justify what you're paying for a shot at them.
The 1st Bowman class, Roman Anthony rookie cards, and how to collect Red Sox legends
Boston has four 1st Bowman cards this year, all likely the cheapest they’ll ever be simply because nobody outside the organization and minor league baseball enthusiasts know most of these names yet. Here's a rough rule of thumb worth keeping in mind: the higher the signing bonus, the more attention collectors tend to pay, and that logic really kicks in once a bonus crosses $750,000. If a front office was willing to bet that kind of money on a teenager's upside, it's a fair question why a collector wouldn't take the same signal seriously.
Dawvris Brito signed for $1.2 million as the headliner of the 2026 international class, a shortstop with quick-twitch athleticism and triple-digit exit velocities already, and if there is a speculative play, I’d be playing in Brito’s camp. Garielvin Silverio signed for $1.4 million as a physical, left-handed-hitting corner outfielder with raw power, but is likely limited to a corner outfield spot due to lack of speed and athleticism.
Louis Andujar is the wild card of the group, and exactly the kind of story that makes chasing a bargain fun. Boston signed him for just $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic, a number so modest he barely registered outside the organization. He quietly hit .280 with a .974 OPS in the Dominican Summer League, then hit .410 with a 1.233 OPS in his stateside debut this year, good enough for FCL Hitter of the Week honors. If the $750,000 rule (that I made up completely) tells you who the industry believes in, Andujar is the opposite bet entirely, a near-free flier already outplaying his price tag.
The last name in this class comes with the best story attached. Enddy Azocar signed with Boston in January 2024 for just $40,000 out of Venezuela. He climbed all the way to the Red Sox's No. 5 prospect by this summer, hitting .286 with 18 home runs and 11 stolen bases in 85 games, right before Boston shipped him to Baltimore in the Rutschman trade. He hasn't missed a beat since, hitting .467 with a 1.238 OPS in his first 15 at-bats for High-A Frederick, and he's now the Orioles' No. 8 prospect. His 1st Bowman card will always have a Red Sox jersey, a snapshot of the last piece of a $40,000 bet Boston made and then dealt away for a franchise catcher.
Connelly Early carries that same wrinkle in a smaller way. Boston shipped him to the Nationals this July in the Curtis Mead deal, yet his Red RC in this release still has him in a Red Sox uniform. If you're a true Red Sox fan who likes owning a piece of the ones that got away, these are exactly those cards.
If you’re a top prospect hunter and have slept on Franklin Arias, this release gives you more chances to buy into his market, just not the way you'd expect. He doesn't get a 1st Bowman card this year (his 1st came last year), but he shows up with a prospect auto and two inserts as one of the sport's top prospects. If his original 1st Bowman wave passed you by, this is a more affordable way back into his market before he's an everyday big leaguer.
If you believe in Roman Anthony, the rest of this checklist is built for you. This year has been riddled with injury, a hand issue that kept him out for months. But zoom out. Boston signed this guy to an eight-year, $130 million extension back in August 2025, running through 2033 with a 2034 option and escalators that could push the value to $230 million.
That's a franchise betting on a 22-year-old being the face of this roster for the next decade, and Anthony's Red RC, Chrome Rookie Auto, Jumbo Chrome Autograph Relic, and Across the Seams autograph all reflect that same belief. If you're the kind of collector who buys into a player rather than a single season, the injury noise shouldn't scare you off so much as it should make this exact window the moment to buy in, before he's healthy and the price reflects it.
Every team in this release gets a shot at the future. Not every team has the history and memories that Red Sox fans have and names like Manny Ramirez, Roger Clemens, and Pedro Martínez in the same checklist should be like a slice of heaven. Ramirez lands in the Bowman Garbage Pail Kids (GPK) insert, a fitting nod to one of the most feared right-handed bats this franchise has ever run out. Clemens goes a step further with a base GPK card and an autograph version, and Pedro shows up in the Final Draft insert. None of these are prospect chases, and none will likely come cheap either, but they're closer to a tribute set than an investment. For a fanbase that grew up on these names, that's a fun thing to pull, regardless of cost.
Prices are always inflated in the first few weeks. Anthony's cards will likely cost the most, so waiting a month for the market to settle isn't unreasonable if you're patient. But Brito, Silverio, Azocar, and Andujar are cheap speculative buys worth grabbing now, and the Manny, Clemens, and Pedro pulls are worth paying up for if the fun of the rip matters more to you than the price tag.

item.content:encoded:
En casi cualquier parque de Grandes Ligas hay una historia dominicana. Puede estar en el lineup, en el bullpen o esperando su turno en el dugouts. La República Dominicana, una pequeña nación del Caribe con menos de 12 millones de habitantes, se convirtió en una de las mayores fábricas de talento del beisbol mundial.
Pedro Martínez, Vladimir Guerrero, Adrián Beltré y David Ortiz son parte de esa historia. También lo son Juan Soto, Fernando Tatis Jr. y Junior Caminero, una generación que mantiene a la isla como uno de los principales proveedores de peloteros para las Grandes Ligas. El año pasado, 144 jugadores dominicanos aparecieron en el Big Show, alrededor del 10 por ciento de todos los peloteros de la liga, de acuerdo con datos recopilados por ProPublica.
Detrás de cada firma existe una industria que comienza mucho antes de que un adolescente pueda ponerse la gorra de un equipo de Grandes Ligas. Entre 2012 y principios de 2026, las organizaciones de MLB pagaron 1,042 millones de dólares en bonos a prospectos dominicanos, de acuerdo con el análisis de ProPublica. Ese dinero alimenta a entrenadores, academias, intermediarios y prestamistas que conocen el sistema desde mucho antes de que el jugador llegue a un estadio de Grandes Ligas.
¿Cómo las mafias se aprovechan de los prospectos?
El problema comienza incluso antes de que exista una firma oficial. Los llamados preacuerdos permiten que equipos y prospectos pacten cantidades con años de anticipación, pese a que los jugadores internacionales no pueden firmar oficialmente hasta cumplir 16 años. Para las familias, el bono que algún día llegará puede convertirse desde mucho antes en una garantía para conseguir dinero inmediato.
Los entrenadores suelen recibir una parte importante del bono por haber formado al jugador, proporcionarle vivienda, alimentación y entrenamiento. ProPublica encontró casos en los que esa comisión llegó al 35 o 50 por ciento. Después aparecen los prestamistas, que entregan dinero a las familias utilizando como garantía una parte del futuro bono.
Una abogada que ha representado a jóvenes peloteros en disputas con entrenadores y prestamistas estimó que 80% de los bonos de Grandes Ligas pagados a prospectos dominicanos tienen algún préstamo asociado. Se calcula que hasta 500 millones de dólares de los 1,042 millones entregados entre 2012 y 2026 podrían terminar rápidamente en manos de entrenadores y prestamistas.
En ese mundo aparece Santo Caraballo. ProPublica lo describe como uno de los prestamistas más conocidos del beisbol dominicano. Su negocio consistía en entregar dinero a familias cuyos hijos tenían un preacuerdo con una organización de Grandes Ligas y cobrar después cantidades mucho mayores, utilizando el futuro bono como garantía. Caraballo defendió el modelo al explicar que el riesgo también estaba de su lado.
“Tú no sabes si se va a dar o no se va a dar, porque si el pelotero no firma, no cobras”, dijo en una entrevista a ProPublica.
Uno de los casos investigados es el de Belfi Rivera, quien a los 14 años llegó a un acuerdo verbal con los Diamondbacks por 1.8 millones de dólares. Cuando llegó el momento de cobrar, 630,000 dólares fueron para su entrenador, John Carmona, por una comisión equivalente al 35%. Más de 950,000 dólares terminaron en manos de Caraballo.
La familia de Belfi, de acuerdo con ProPublica, recibió inicialmente alrededor de 25,000 dólares. Los padres afirmaron que Caraballo les prestó ese dinero a cambio de recibir una cantidad mucho mayor cuando llegara el bono. La familia tenía poca experiencia financiera y, según el reportaje, ni siquiera recibió una copia del contrato que firmó.
Pero el nombre que hizo todavía más atractiva aquella relación fue el de David Ortiz.
Los padres de Belfi dijeron a ProPublica que Caraballo se presentó como la “mano derecha” de Ortiz. La reputación de Big Papi, una de las figuras más reconocidas de la historia reciente del beisbol dominicano, ayudó a generar confianza en una familia que estaba entrando por primera vez a un mundo en el que se manejaban cientos de miles de dólares.
Después, según los padres, Caraballo les habló de la posibilidad de invertir el dinero que todavía recibirían de los Diamondbacks en un negocio relacionado con él y Ortiz.
“Yo me puse contento porque ya mi muchacho va a tener una gente que le puede dar un consejo”, contó Eduardo Rivera a ProPublica.
La relación entre Ortiz y Caraballo no era una invención. Registros corporativos de Florida muestran que en 2021 ambos estuvieron vinculados con Big Papi Sports Group, una empresa que fue disuelta al año siguiente. Ortiz reconoció ante ProPublica que había invertido millones de dólares en el negocio de beisbol de Caraballo, aunque no precisó cuánto dinero ni identificó la empresa.
Ortiz aseguró que su relación empresarial con Caraballo estaba limitada a préstamos para entrenadores y que no trabajaba directamente con los padres de los prospectos porque recuperar ese dinero resultaba complicado. Sin embargo, ProPublica encontró un documento judicial en el que aparece el nombre de Ortiz en un contrato firmado con los padres de un jugador de 13 años.
El acuerdo establecía que Ortiz y Caraballo proporcionarían al menor alimentación, vivienda, estudios, entrenamiento, ropa, suplementos y oportunidades para ser observado por scouts. A cambio, recibirían 35% de su eventual bono de firma.
El jugador nunca firmó con una organización de Grandes Ligas y la demanda relacionada con el acuerdo fue desechada por cuestiones procesales. El documento, sin embargo, muestra que al menos en un caso el nombre de Ortiz sí apareció directamente en un contrato relacionado con un menor y con el futuro bono de un prospecto.
La investigación también documentó que Caraballo utilizaba la relación con Ortiz como parte de su capital de confianza. Padres, entrenadores y abogados consultados por ProPublica dijeron que el prestamista mencionaba al al Miembro del Salón de la Fama durante sus negocios.
Ortiz, por su parte, rechazó haber autorizado ese uso de su nombre.
“Yo nunca autoricé a Santo Caraballo a usar mi nombre o mi reputación para ganar la confianza de jóvenes peloteros o sus familias, para promover préstamos o inversiones, o para representar transacciones financieras como si fueran personalmente respaldadas por mí”, cito el reportaje por medio de un documento compartido por el abogado de Ortiz.
“Yo nunca participaría a sabiendas en ninguna operación que tenga la intención de tomar ventaja de un joven jugador o su familia”, extendió la cita.
Ortiz dijo además que comenzó a alejarse de Caraballo después de observar conductas que consideró inapropiadas. Según su declaración, la relación empresarial “comenzó a llegar a su fin” hace más de 18 meses y la relación personal terminó aproximadamente entre un año y medio y dos años antes de sus declaraciones a ProPublica.
La investigación, sin embargo, encontró una imagen que complica esa cronología. En septiembre de 2025, Ortiz y Caraballo viajaron juntos en un avión privado rumbo a Puerto Rico para asistir a un concierto de Bad Bunny.
La batalla de Ortiz en la disputa laboral de 2022
En 2022, MLB y el Sindicato de Jugadores negociaban un nuevo contrato colectivo y uno de los puntos más importantes era la posibilidad de establecer un draft internacional. La propuesta habría eliminado los preacuerdos que permiten a equipos y jugadores pactar cantidades antes de la edad oficial para firmar.
MLB defendía el draft como una manera de terminar con ese sistema. El sindicato se oponía porque consideraba que limitaría la capacidad de los prospectos para elegir equipo y eliminaría la competencia entre organizaciones que ayuda a elevar los bonos.
Ortiz intervino públicamente en favor de rechazar el draft. En un mensaje de voz dirigido a jugadores y entrenadores dominicanos, pidió organizar una campaña de oposición.
“Si permitimos que el draft suceda aquí en la República Dominicana, hasta sus tataranietos, y todos los demás, se verán afectados por él”, dijo Ortiz, según el audio obtenido por ProPublica. “Si dejamos que nos impongan eso aquí, estaremos en graves problemas”.
El draft no fue incluido finalmente en el acuerdo entre MLB y el sindicato.
Cuando ProPublica preguntó directamente a Ortiz si su oposición estaba relacionada con sus intereses empresariales junto a Caraballo, el exjugador no respondió y terminó la llamada.
Posteriormente, a través de su abogado, Ortiz negó que existiera una motivación económica detrás de su postura.
“Mi oposición a la propuesta de la liga nunca estuvo motivada por intereses personales”, señaló.
Según el comunicado, su postura estaba basada en sus opiniones sobre el desarrollo de los peloteros dominicanos y en el impacto que, a su juicio, tendría un draft internacional sobre el beisbol en el país.
El reportaje de ProPublica no establece que Ortiz haya cometido personalmente fraude o usura, ni que haya cobrado directamente los préstamos de los jóvenes. Documenta una relación empresarial y personal con Caraballo, un prestamista que obtuvo importantes cantidades de dinero de bonos de prospectos dominicanos.

item.content:encoded:
Baseball is everywhere in the Dominican Republic, which sends a disproportionate number of players to the American major and minor leagues, including Hall of Famers like Pedro Martínez and Adrian Beltré. Playing fields and training academies dot the country in villages where players who’ve made the leap to the pros are immortalized in murals.
For nearly half a century, the Dominican Republic has sent more players to the majors than any country outside the United States. The nation, which has a population roughly that of Ohio’s, had 144 players reach the major leagues last year. That’s about 10% of the league.
The Dominican baseball factory is a volume business, with teams paying signing bonuses to about 450 prospects each year. Fewer than 10% of those young players will ever see a single pitch in the majors, but in a country as impoverished as the Dominican Republic those bonuses — worth several times the country’s average annual income — could be life-changing for the players and their families. Yet Major League Baseball has long allowed a corrosive system to fester that rigs the game against young players in favor of opportunistic trainers and predatory moneylenders.
Here are the key highlights of ProPublica’s investigation into the Dominican baseball system.
Trainers coach children in exchange for future earnings.
Young baseball players in the United States and Canada must enter the major league system through its annual draft of young prospects. But in the Dominican Republic it’s a free-for-all, with players going to the highest bidder.
After MLB scouts began to recognize the Dominican Republic as a source of cheap talent, teams opened bare-bones training academies to develop young players. Eventually, the buscones — men relied on by teams to identify local talent — realized they could start their own academies. There are now hundreds of such facilities and, according to a national trade association, approximately 6,000 trainers.
In addition to coaching, the trainers who operate these academies generally provide room, board and equipment. Education often falls by the wayside. In return, they receive a share — typically 35% to 50% — of a player’s signing bonus. Most of those bonuses are valued at around $30,000, but they can be as high as six or seven figures.
From 2012 through the beginning of 2026, major league teams paid Dominican prospects $1.042 billion in bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis. But much of that money — up to half a billion dollars — is almost immediately siphoned off by trainers and lenders.
To get around league rules, MLB teams make handshake deals with underage players.
Major league rules bar teams from making official deals with players under the age of 16, but teams have long circumvented this ban through the use of unwritten early agreements, or preacuerdos. In these handshake deals, typically arranged through a player’s trainer, the team pledges to pay a certain amount to the player once he is of legal age to be signed.
With players as young as 11 involved in such deals, it can be years before the prospect receives his bonus.
Moneylenders persuade families to sign over players’ bonuses for high-interest loans.
Preacuerdos and the lure of these promised payouts have created a cottage industry of prestamistas, or moneylenders, who persuade players’ families to sign away portions of these impending bonuses in exchange for loans with sky-high interest rates.
The Dominican Republic repealed its usury laws 24 years ago. High-interest lenders advertise online, targeting young ballplayers and their families. One WhatsApp ad touted loans for “baseball players who have agreements.”
Belfi Rivera was 14 when he made a handshake deal with the Arizona Diamondbacks that would pay him $1.8 million after he turned 16. (The Diamondbacks did not respond to a request for comment.) Ultimately, he’d see very little of that money. The trainer who had brokered the deal got his share, worth $630,000. More than $950,000 went to someone who had no hand in teaching Belfi how to play baseball: Santo Caraballo, a lender who formed a business partnership with  Red Sox legend and Hall of Famer David Ortiz.
In a statement sent through his lawyer, Ortiz said that his business relationship with Caraballo “began to come to an end” more than 18 months ago.” He added that he ended his personal relationship with Caraballo “a year and a half to two years ago” after “noticing conduct by Mr. Caraballo that I considered inappropriate. I started distancing myself from him personally and placed the relevant matters in the hands of my legal advisors.”  
However, in September 2025, Ortiz and Caraballo filmed themselves heading for Puerto Rico on a private jet, drinking and dancing on their way to a Bad Bunny concert.
In a brief conversation, Caraballo told ProPublica that his business was not the biggest or “that lucrative.” He added that the risk in loaning money to families is that “you never know if it will succeed or not because if the player doesn’t get signed, you don’t get paid.” Multiple attempts were made to reach him again, including sending him a summary of ProPublica’s findings. He never responded.
One lender used a player’s deadly car crash to start his empire.
Before becoming a fixture in the prestamista sphere and partnering with Ortiz, Caraballo played a shadowy role in salvaging the career of rising MLB prospect Oneil Cruz. In 2020, while Cruz was a player in the Pittsburgh Pirates’ minor league system, he crashed his Jeep into the back of a motorcycle, killing three people. Prosecutors initially said the ballplayer had been drinking, and he faced the possibility of three years in prison. According to numerous interviews and court records, Caraballo was brought in by Cruz’s parents and negotiated payments to the victims’ families. In exchange, they signed agreements withdrawing all claims against Cruz, who is currently the starting center fielder for the Pirates. The case against Cruz, who denied any wrongdoing, was dismissed. ProPublica made numerous attempts to reach Caraballo about his role, including sending him a summary of our findings. He never responded.
Cruz declined a request for an interview. His lawyer, Amauris Vásquez Disla, called the accident “a profound tragedy for all parties involved, especially the victims’ families.” He went on to say that the court “issued an order of dismissal based on the findings, a legally binding decision that was a lawful resolution of this matter.”
A spokesperson for the Pittsburgh Pirates said the team and Cruz “addressed this matter more than six years ago based on the information available and the outcome of the legal proceedings.”
That lender then partnered with the Dominican Republic’s biggest baseball star.
By 2021, records show that Caraballo and Ortiz had entered into a business partnership, with both men listed on corporation records of a Florida company called Big Papi Sports Group. The company was dissolved the next year. What, if anything, it did is not clear. Their financial and personal relationships, however, continued. Ortiz acknowledged to a ProPublica reporter that he had invested millions of dollars into Caraballo’s baseball business. He added that his business with Caraballo was limited to making loans to trainers, not kids. At Ortiz’s 2022 Hall of Fame induction ceremony, Caraballo sat with the retired player’s family.
Why did David Ortiz oppose an international draft?
Ortiz’s connection to Caraballo doesn’t just spotlight the power and influence that these moneylenders can attain in the Dominican Republic. It also raises questions about the Red Sox legend’s involvement in persuading major league players to oppose an international draft.
For more than a decade, MLB commissioner Rob Manfred has made the case in favor of a draft for prospects from Latin America. Last year, during a visit to the Dominican Republic, he acknowledged that preacuerdos were “problematic” and argued that the “best solution to early deals is a draft.” Manfred and supporters of an international draft say it would make early agreements impossible.
The players union has opposed such a draft, arguing that it would restrict a prospect’s ability to choose his employer and eliminate bidding wars that drive up bonuses. The union has acknowledged that the Dominican system of early deals is troubled but has maintained for years that this is due to the league not enforcing its own rules.
During contract negotiations in 2022, the league was again pushing for an international draft, and the issue had become a major sticking point. But then, said people on both sides of the discussions, Ortiz got involved, sending a voice message to Dominican players and trainers, declaring a “red alert.”
Listen to Our “Paper Trail” Podcast
“If we allow the draft to happen here in the Dominican Republic, even your great-great-grandchildren, and everyone else’s, will be affected by it,” Ortiz said, according to an audio copy of the message obtained by ProPublica. “If we let them push that thing through here, we’ll be in deep trouble.”
In the message, Ortiz shared the phone number for Tony Clark, the union’s executive director, and urged everybody to express their opposition to the draft. What he didn’t share was that he had a financial interest in preserving the system.
When asked over the phone if his opposition to the draft had anything to do with his partnership with Caraballo, who profits from the current system, Ortiz didn’t answer and hung up shortly afterward.
In a subsequent statement sent through his lawyer, Ortiz said his position regarding the international draft “was never motivated by personal interests.” The statement went on to say that his opposition “was based on my views regarding the development of Dominican players and the impact I believed such a system would have on baseball in our country.”
“Major League Baseball knows how dirty the business is here.”
Major League Baseball is a formidable economic and political presence in the Dominican Republic. But outside of the league’s push for an international draft, it’s done nothing that would put an end to or reform the early agreement system. It has never publicly warned or penalized a team for making an early deal, and its attempts to educate families about moneylenders have been ineffectual. A spokesperson for MLB declined to comment and referred to past statements by league officials calling for an overhaul of the Dominican system.
“Major League Baseball knows how dirty the business is here,” said Piñao Ortiz, who was the Dominican commissioner of baseball from 1996 to 2000, “but it’s not doing anything to stop it.”

item.content:encoded:
BOSTON (WHDH) - Red Sox rookie Payton Tolle Sunday became just the sixth pitcher in MLB history to throw an immaculate inning in the first inning of a game. An immaculate inning occurs when a pitcher records three strikeouts on nine pitches.
The 23-year-old lefty has quickly become a fan favorite through not only his pitching prowess, but by showcasing his infectious personality. On the eighth pitch of the inning, Tolle flashed a bright smile into the Red Sox dugout before getting Kansas City Royals right fielder Jac Caglianone to strikeout swinging, completing the rare feat.
“We saw him smile towards the end and…said ‘oh my gosh it’s almost immaculate inning,’ and then he got it. And we were just floored,” said Caroline Stacey, a Red Sox fan from Maine. “Tolle is such a great player, he’s so fun to watch. Like, everything he does is just fun so it was really great to see him celebrate and have such an amazing accomplishment.”
The last Red Sox player to throw an immaculate inning at the start of a game was Hall-of-Famer Pedro Martinez in 2002. The then-30-year-old struck out three Mariners in a row on May 18.
“Unbelievable. Eighth in the history of the Red Sox is, I mean, unbelievable,” said Chris Molina, a Red Sox fan visiting Boston from Kansas.
After the game, Tolle said he hopes to ignite the team in any way he can.
“Trying to be the spark in whatever way I can. If that’s pitching or that’s offense, just trying to find that way is kind of what I want to do,” he explained.
It’s that spark that has him winning over the city of Boston as well as his teammates. Red Sox star outfielder Roman Anthony praised Tolle during an on field interview after the game on NESN.
“You see the amount of people that are behind him, and the energy he brings to Red Sox baseball and the city of Boston,” Anthony said. “Everyone around, they ride for him, and we feel that energy when he’s on the bump the minute he takes it. He’s such an amazing person, and an amazing teammate who’s there for us every single day, and whether he’s pitching or not he brings that energy. So it’s so fun to be behind him. He’s amazing.”
The manager of the Red Sox Team Store says they can barely keep his jersey stocked on the shelves as the demand has become so high.
“When you combine the talent that he has with the personality that he has – we’ve seen this before with certain guys like Johnny Damon, David Ortiz, who were big personalities and great players – I mean, that means he’s going to be a star for years to come,” said Tim Pettit, Manager of the Red Sox Team Store.
Following the immaculate inning, Tolle went on to throw five more scoreless innings, finishing with seven strikeouts. The Red Sox went on to beat the Royals 4-1 and secure the series win.

item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — Boston Red Sox left-hander Payton Tolle pitched an immaculate inning to open Sunday’s game against the Kansas City Royals.
The 23-year-old left-hander threw a called third strike past Nick Loftin, then got Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone swinging in the nine-pitch inning.
Tolle became Boston’s first pitcher to throw an immaculate inning opening a game since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez at Fenway Park against Seattle on May 18, 2002.
“It was pretty cool. It was a pretty cool feeling,” Tolle said after the Red Sox beat the Royals 4-1 to win the series. “That was the first time, I think in high school I might have had a couple of opportunities at it. That was fun, that was cool.”
Caglianone was the only one to get his bat on a ball, fouling his first pitch to the left side.
When Tolle got two strikes on Caglianone, most of the fans rose and cheered loudly. Tolle pumped a fist when the strikeout and inning were complete after looking over at the dugout with a bit of a smile before the last pitch.
“I was definitely thinking about it,” he said. “I looked over at (pitching coach Andrew Bailey) and he was smiling, too.”
It was Boston’s eighth immaculate inning, the second in the first inning and the sixth in MLB recorded history to open the game. Hall of Famer Sandy Koufax had the first recorded one on June 30, 1962.
Chris Sale had the most recent for the Red Sox on Aug. 26, 2021, at Fenway against Minnesota.
Tolle went six scoreless innings with seven strikeouts and allowed four singles.

item.content:encoded:
Los Red Sox tuvieron que retrasar dos veces el inicio del juego del domingo debido a la lluvia que azotó Boston en el cierre de la semana. Fue imposible jugar antes de las 4:55 de la tarde, casi cuatro horas después de lo inicialmente estipulado porque iba a ser un domingo normal con el primer pitcheo lanzándose a la 1:35 de la tarde.
En la medida que se acercaban las 3:00 p.m iba despejándose la duda de que tampoco a esa hora iba a iniciar el duelo entre los patirojos y los Reales de Kansas City. En todo caso, el pitcher Payton Tolle se acercó a su manager Chad Tracy, le hizo un saludo militar y le dijo que estaría listo a la hora que el partido comenzara.
El zurdo no estaba mintiendo. A las 4:55 p.m tiró una recta de 95 millas en strike. Ocho envíos después consiguió una hazaña que solo ocho miembros del club habían conseguido. El monticulista tiró ocho rectas y un sinker para ponchar a sus tres primeros rivales con nueve strikes en fila y convertirse en el octavo miembro de la franquicia en lograr un inning inmaculado.
Es el segundo que lo consigue en el primer inning uniéndose al legendario Pedro Martínez.
“Fue divertido”, celebró Tolle después de la victoria de 4 a 1. “Fue chévere. Creo que después del tercer strike me vino la idea a la cabeza. Pero eso no debería pasar. Creo que debería ser mejor y no andar pensando en esas cosas, pero así sucedió”.
La transmisión del equipo captó el momento previo al último envío antes de la hazaña. Tolle miró a su dugout y sonrió. Dio cuenta que estaba al tanto de lo estaba por suceder en conchupancia con su coach de pitcheo Andrew Bailey.
“Estaba definitivamente pensando en eso”, contó. “Lo tenía en mente. Creo que miré a “Bales” y estaba sonriendo también. Fue divertido”.
Solo ocho monticulistas de los Red Sox habían conseguido esa gesta. El último había sido Chris Sale en mayo de 2021.
“Fue impresionante”, agregó el primera base Willson Contreras, quien regresó a la acción después de casi dos semanas lesionado. “Estuvo atacando la zona de strike. No estaba permitiendo mucha gente en base. Creo que es la primera vez que soy parte de algo así”.
Payton Tolle siguió brillando después de la hazaña y terminó con seis innings completos, sin permitir carreras, un bateador golpeado, cuatro hits y siete ponches.
Y si les quedó alguna duda sobre el saludo militar, tal parece es una broma que se gasta con Tracy todos los días.
“Tiene haciéndolo desde que llegué acá”, bromeó Tracy. “No le pedí que lo hiciera. Solo lo hace. No necesito que lo haga, pero es Tolle y eso es lo que hace”.

item.content:encoded:
Tolle mimics Pedro in immaculate first inning ... with more smiles
This browser does not support the video element.
This story was excerpted from Ian Browne’s Red Sox Beat newsletter. To read the full newsletter, click here. And subscribe to get it regularly in your inbox.
BOSTON – It was more than 24 years ago, and I was in my first year covering the Red Sox for MLB.com, and everyone in the press box, the stands and even the two dugouts at Fenway Park were feeling a little restless. That’s what happens when you sit through a two-hour and five-minute rain delay waiting for the game to start.
But Pedro Martínez had a way of making everything worth the wait.
So when Payton Tolle threw his immaculate first inning on Sunday – after a rain delay of nearly two hours – my mind immediately flashed back to May 18, 2002.
Feats like this, these rare milestone moments, are what set baseball apart.
I’ve seen two no-hitters, plus at least four cycles I remember off the top of my head, and countless other unforgettable moments.
The one thing I’ve still never seen live is a perfect game. Here’s hoping I’ll get to witness that someday.
Though I had a scheduled day off on Sunday and wasn’t in my press box perch to witness Tolle becoming the sixth Red Sox pitcher in history to throw an immaculate inning, I immediately flashed back to Martínez against the Mariners on that soggy Saturday nearly a quarter century ago.
Of the eight times on record that Red Sox pitchers have thrown immaculate innings (including three times by Chris Sale), Tolle and Martínez are the only two who started a game by doing so.
Martínez’s day started with the ultimate challenge – facing Ichiro Suzuki. The Seattle hit king was in just his second year stateside, but already a legend.
But he wasn’t ready for Martínez’s first two pitches – a pair of high fastballs which both went for called strikes. The third pitch was a changeup that Suzuki weakly waved through. Seldom had he looked so overmatched on a swing before or after that.
Mark McLemore was up next, and swung through a first-pitch curveball. Then he fouled off a fastball. And looked at a fastball on the outside corner to become Martínez’s second victim.
Ruben Sierra was all that stood between Martínez and what wound up being the only immaculate inning of his Hall of Fame career. Sierra watched a cutter go by for a strike, and looked at a fastball next to make it 0-2.
This browser does not support the video element.
At this point, the Fenway Park crowd stood as one.
“The crowd is standing already, in the first inning,” Red Sox radio play-by-play man Joe Castiglione, a sound of surprise in his voice, informed his audience.
When Martínez got Sierra to fish for a high fastball, the roar was instantaneous.
“That gave us a huge lift,” Boston’s Brian Daubach said after the game. “Running in from left field after the inning, I was like, 'All right, now we’ve got a game.’”
The Red Sox went on to win, 4-1, as Martinez improved to 10-0 against the Mariners with a 0.94 ERA covering 77 innings. Keep in mind that the Mariners of the late 90s and early 2000s were one of the best teams in the game.
While Tolle didn’t face that stiff of an opponent in the Royals, he did go through one of the best players in the game in Bobby Witt Jr. to accomplish his feat. Kansas City’s No. 2 hitter, Witt waved through three straight fastballs between 97 and 98 mph as the second punchout of the first inning.
One of the indelible moments from Tolle’s immaculate frames: the huge grin that spread across his face almost unconsciously between pitches eight and nine. He knew what he was on the verge of doing and soaked in the moment.
Martínez? He never smiled on the mound. He couldn’t compete and have fun at the same time, like Tolle has the unique ability to do.
As different as their personalities are, they are now forever linked in Red Sox history.

item.content:encoded:
El lanzador zurdo de los Boston Red Sox, Payton Tolle, logró una entrada inmaculada para abrir el partido del domingo contra los Kansas City Royals.
El zurdo de 23 años ponchó a Nick Loftin con un tercer strike cantado y luego retiró a Bobby Witt Jr. y a Jac Caglianone por la vía del strikeout tirándole, todo ello en una entrada de nueve lanzamientos.
Tolle se convirtió en el primer lanzador de Boston en lograr una entrada inmaculada al inicio de un partido desde que lo hiciera el miembro del Salón de la Fama Pedro Martínez en Fenway Park contra Seattle, el 18 de mayo de 2002.
"Fue genial. Fue una sensación increíble", dijo Tolle después de que los Red Sox vencieran a los Royals 4-1 para llevarse la serie. "Fue la primera vez; creo que tal vez tuve un par de oportunidades de lograrlo en la secundaria. Fue divertido, fue genial".
Caglianone fue el único que logró hacer contacto con la pelota, enviando su primer lanzamiento de foul hacia el lado izquierdo.
Cuando Tolle acumuló dos strikes contra Caglianone, la mayoría de los aficionados se puso de pie y vitoreó con fuerza. Tolle celebró con un gesto de puño en alto al concretarse el ponche y finalizar la entrada, tras haber mirado hacia el dugout con una leve sonrisa antes del último lanzamiento.
"Definitivamente estaba pensando en ello", comentó. "Miré hacia donde estaba (el entrenador de lanzadores Andrew Bailey) y él también sonreía".
Fue la octava entrada inmaculada en la historia de Boston, la segunda lograda en el primer episodio y la sexta registrada en la historia de la MLB al inicio de un partido. Sandy Koufax, miembro del Salón de la Fama, protagonizó la primera registrada el 30 de junio de 1962.
Chris Sale había logrado la más reciente para los Red Sox el 26 de agosto de 2021, en Fenway Park y frente a Minnesota.
Tolle lanzó seis entradas en blanco, ponchó a siete bateadores y permitió cuatro sencillos.

Payton Tolle starts with immaculate inning, Roman Anthony gets key hit as Red Sox beat Royals 4-1
The host team defeated the visiting club four to one; the starting pitcher opened the game with an immaculate inning
- 1 minuto de lectura'
BOSTON (AP) — Payton Tolle opened the game with an immaculate inning , Roman Anthony hit a go-ahead single and the Boston Red Sox beat the Kansas City Royals 4-1 on Sunday in a game that’s start was delayed by rain.
Tolle is the first Boston pitcher to throw an immaculate inning (three strikeouts on nine pitches) to start a game since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez did it on May 18, 2002.
Caleb Durbin hit a solo homer and Trevor Story added a game-breaking two-run single for the Red Sox, who took the final two games of the three-game series.
Carter Jensen drove in the Royals’ run with a pinch-hit single. Kansas City was looking for its first series win in Boston since 2017.
In the seventh, Anthony lined an opposite-field single against reliever Connor Thomas after Craig Kimbrel (1-5) walked the first two batters.
Garrett Whitlock (7-1) was credited with the victory. Aroldis Chapman got the final three outs for his 34th save and the 401st of his career.
Tolle, a hard-throwing 23-year-old left-hander, fanned Nick Loftin called, then got Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone swinging in the first.
He went six scoreless innings, striking out seven while allowing four singles.
Noah Cameron gave up a run over six sharp innings.
Durbin belted Cameron’s first pitch into the first row of seats above the Green Monster. Story’s single came off Nate Pearson in the eighth.
Jensen’s RBI single inside the first-base bag tied it.
The club announced Saturday that the finale's start time was pushed back 90 minutes due to the forecast of rain, which came and delayed the first pitch by 1 hour, 50 minutes.
Up next
Royals: RHP Michael Wacha (9-8, 3.25 ERA) is scheduled for the opener of a three-game series in Houston on Tuesday.
Red Sox: LHP Patrick Sandoval (1-5, 4.58) starts Tuesday in the series opener against Texas.
